## 1.2 Programming Basics

A ==Scanner== is a text parser that can get numbers, words, or phrases from an input source.
`Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);`
System.out.println starts a new output line after the outputted values, called a newline. Note: it is after, not before.

## 1.3 Comments and whitespace

- Use blank lines to separate conceptually distinct statements.
- Indent lines the same amount.
- Align items to reduce visual clutter. Like with comments

![](data:image/png;base64,)

- Use a single space before and after any operators like =, +, * or / to make statements more readable.
## 1.4 Errors and warnings

Syntax errors for missing semicolons typically occur in the line AFTER the typo because that is where the compiler gets confused.

Even for things other than missing semicolons, if you cannot find an error on the reported line, look at PREVIOUS lines since this is common for other errors.

If multiple errors get reported, focus on fixing just the first error and then compiling. The remaining error messages are commonly due to the first error. Even if they are not, it is just easier to not get confused.

Because a syntax error is detected by the compiler, it is known as a type of compile-time error.

A logic error, also called a bug, is an error that occurs while a program runs.

For example, the intended operation could be numBeans * numJars but is accidentally typed as numBeans + numJars

A warning is a suggestion to streamline code or a possible runtime error. By default, Java compilers don't print every possible warning. Javac can be run as javac -xlint yourfile.java to enable all recommended warnings.

## 1.5 Computers and programs (general)

Tiny switches controlled electronically by positive/negative volts are the foundation of computers. Like a light switch but teeny tiny and you don't have to switch it by hand.

Positive voltage is treated as a 1 and a zero voltage as a 0. These are known as bits (binary digits).

They build connections of switches, known as circuits, to perform calculations.

To support different calculations, circuits called processors were created to process (aka execute) a list of desired calculations, with each calculation called an instruction.

Instructions are stored in a memory. A memory is a circuit that can store 0s and 1s in each of a series of thousands of addressed locations.

So a computer is basically a processor interacting with a memory.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The programmer-created sequence of instructions is called a program, application, or app.

It starts by executing the instruction at location 0, then 1, then 2, etc.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

REALLY HELPFUL. The magenta is the stated instructions, under it is the actions performed, and the right is where info is retrieved/stored from.

Instructions represented as 0s and 1s are known as machine instructions, and a sequence of them together forms an executable program (sometimes just called an executable).

An assembler is a program that automatically translates human readable instructions, known as assembly language instructions, into machine instructions.

In the 1960s and 1970s, programmers created high-level languages to support programming using formulas or algorithms, so a programmer could write something like: F = (9 / 5) * C + 32.

To support high-level languages, programmers created compilers, which are programs that automatically translate high-level language programs into executable programs.

Using a virtual processor to process executables on multiple processor types is sometimes called bytecode. The real processor runs a program, the virtual machine, that executes the instructions in the bytecode. Makes programs slower but is portable and versatile.

## 1.6 Computer Tour

A disk stores files and data in a non-volatile nature. They do this by orientating magnetic particles in a 0 or 1 position. It spins under a head that pulses electricity to orient the particles. Flash storage devices can do the same except they do so by tunneling electrons into special circuits on the memory's chip and removing them with a "flash" of electricity that draws them back out.

RAM (random-access memory) temporarily holds data and is designed such that any address can be accessed much faster than disk. (a few clock ticks vs a few hundred). It is volatile, losing its contents when powered off.

The first program a processor (CPU)  runs is commonly called the BIOS (basic input/output system), which sets up the computer's basic peripherals. Then it does the OS. A processor may contain a small amount of RAM for speed, called cache memory, accessible in one clock tick for maintaining a copy of the most-used instructions/data.

A processor's instructions are execute at a rate governed by the processor's clock, which ticks at a specific frequency. From 1MHz (million ticks/second)(cheap 1$ used in microwaves or washing machines) to 1 GHz (billion ticks/second)(10-100$). Each tick is about one action. Computers run multiple programs at once, so OS's will run a little of program A, then a little of B, etc, switching thousands of times a second. (pretty sure multiple cores fixes that)

Transistors were tiny switches integrated onto a single chip called an integrated circuit, or IC.

They continue to get smaller, leading to Moore's Law: the double of IC capacity roughly every 18 months, which continued for several decades. (he actually said 2 years but its actually 18 months from data). In 1971, the first single-IC processor has 2,300 transistors. By 2012, a single IC had several billion transistors containing multiple processors (each called a core)

## 1.7 Language History

- 1978: Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs published a book on a new high-level language named C. It became the dominant language from 1980s-1990s.
- 1985: Bjarne Stroustrup published a book on C++, adding constructs to C to support object-oriented programming.
- 1991: James Gosling and a team at Sun Microsystems (acquired by Oracle in 2010) began developing Java. It had a C/C++ style and was intended to be executable on different types of processors.
- 1995: First public release of Java.
